tagline.text: A small island in Zambales ringed with white sand, just 10 minutes away by boat

children.text: A small, roughly 7.5-hectare island floating off the coast of Candelaria in northern Zambales. It's little more than 10 minutes away by boat from the mainland, and with its white sand, clear water, and shaded camping spots, it's known as "Zambales' little Boracay."
Potipot Island is a small island about
1km

off the Uacon coast of Candelaria in northern Zambales province. It covers about 7.5 hectares, small enough to walk all the way around in under an hour at a leisurely pace. Fine white sand runs along the island's edge, while tall trees crowd the interior, casting cool shade even at midday.

Unlike the gray, ash-laden beaches of southern Zambales, built up from Mount Pinatubo's eruption, Potipot in the north stands out for its fine white sand. The water is shallow and clear, so the sea off the island shifts from emerald to deep blue in bands, with the ridgeline of the Zambales Mountains unfolding like a screen to the east. The island is run by a private caretaker who admits visitors, and without large resorts or rows of shops — just a few nipa huts and a campsite — it stays relatively unspoiled.
It's a long way from Manila, about
5–7 hours

by bus, but that distance also keeps it quieter than the capital's closer beaches, even on weekends. The island has no electricity, with a generator lighting it only at night, making it a good place to unwind away from city noise.

It suits families with children, travelers trying island camping for the first time, and anyone who wants an easy swim at a short-hop island. The boat ride is much shorter than to the rougher southern Zambales coast, so it's also easy on anyone worried about seasickness.
Walk the full loop of the island along its white sand shore. The seaward side is wide open, while the shore facing the mainland gives you a view of the mountains, so the scenery changes as you go.

The water around the island stays waist-deep in many spots even far from shore, making it easy to wade in with children. Depth shifts with the tide, so also enjoy the wide sandbanks that appear at low tide.
Entrance fees often include
1 hour
of free kayak use per group. Paddle around the island in the calm morning and you can see straight down through the water to the sand and sea grass below.

Bring your own tent or rent one on-site and pitch it in the shade of the trees inside the island. At night, once the generator lights go out, only the sound of waves and starlight remain, giving you the feeling of having the whole island to yourself.
The island's west beach faces straight out over the South China Sea, giving you a clear view of the sunset. On clear days in the dry season, sky and sea turn orange together.
Not far from the island's boat landing, Lake Uacon is often ranked as the cleanest lake in central Luzon. Restaurants along its shore serve freshwater fish, and you can rent a boat or kayak there.

Before heading out to the island, stop by the roadside market in Uacon. Freshly caught fish, vegetables, and seasonal fruit are cheap, and in mango season, piles of Zambales' famous carabao mangoes make it easy to stock up on barbecue supplies all in one place.

A day trip is possible, but since it's more than 5 hours from Manila one way, it's best to plan for a night on the island or a night at a beach resort on the mainland.
Take a bus to Santa Cruz, Zambales from the Victory Liner terminal in Cubao, Pasay, or Caloocan, Manila. It takes about
5–7 hours
, with a one-way fare of around
. Tell the conductor in advance that you're getting off at Uacon, Candelaria.
From the Uacon roadside to the boat landing for Potipot, it's about
5–15 minutes
by tricycle, around
per person. There's paid parking near the landing.
From the landing to the island, it takes about
5–10 minutes
by outrigger boat. The round-trip fare runs around
per boat depending on group size, and on the way back you call the landing from the island to send a boat over.
Take the NLEX and SCTEX to Subic or Olongapo, then follow the Zambales coastal road north through Iba. It takes about
5–6 hours
, or about
1 hour 30 minutes–2 hours
from Alaminos if you're coming down from Pangasinan.
The nearest international airport is Clark International Airport (CRK), about
4–5 hours
away by car. By public transport, you'll need to transfer to a Santa Cruz-bound bus in Olongapo.
The
November–May
dry season is best.
December–February
brings cool breezes that make camping comfortable, while
March–May
has the calmest sea and clearest water, though midday temperatures climb close to

. Nipa huts fill up early on Holy Week and summer-break weekends, so book ahead. The mountain range shields the Zambales west coast from the northeast monsoon (Amihan), so the sea stays calm on many days even in
December–February
, making this a good alternative when islands on the east coast turn rough with waves.
June–October

is the rainy season, when the southwest monsoon blows straight in off the sea, and the Zambales coast gets some of the heaviest rain in the Philippines. On high-wave days, boats don't run and the island sometimes closes. During this season, pick a clear day for a day trip, and postpone your plans if a typhoon is forecast.

On the island, you stay in a rented nipa hut or your own tent. Some huts come with a mat and a fan, but electricity only runs at night from a generator, and phone charging is limited and paid. There are toilets and showers, but they're basic. If you'd rather sleep comfortably, it's a good idea to stay at a beach resort in Uacon or along the nearby coast (about

per night) and visit the island as a day trip. Many travelers who do stay overnight leave their car and most of their luggage at a mainland resort and head to the island with only the essentials. Some resorts can arrange a boat connection to the island, so ask when you book.

The island has no restaurant, or only very limited food service, so bringing your own food is the rule. Buy rice, pork and chicken for grilling, fish, and fruit at the roadside market in Uacon, and pack plenty of ice in a cooler. Most nipa huts let you use a barbecue grill. On the way back, you can try freshwater dishes like tilapia at restaurants around Lake Uacon, and in
April–May
, be sure to pick up some Zambales mangoes, famous for their sweetness.
The island accepts cash only. Bring enough cash for the entrance fee, boat fare, and hut rental.
There are only a few nipa huts, and they fill up fast on peak-season weekends. If you're staying overnight, contact the management in advance to reserve one.
Get the boat landing's contact number for your return trip, and go easy on your phone battery.
Bring at least 3 liters of drinking water per person per day, along with a power bank and a lantern.
Even with plenty of shade from the trees, the sun on the sand is strong. Bring reef-safe sunscreen and a rash guard.
Taking all your trash back with you is the rule. Bring several large trash bags.
The bus back to Manila is a roadside flag-down, so seats can run out on weekend afternoons. Don't leave it too late.
The island is small enough to see it all in half a day. Plan a relaxed schedule of reading in the shade or napping in a hammock for the most satisfying trip. Bring a hammock and a mat.
If you're combining this with Hundred Islands or Bolinao, an efficient west-coast loop is 3 days, 2 nights — one night in the Pangasinan area, one night at Potipot.
The island has no lifeguard on duty. Even in shallow water, keep an eye on children at all times, and don't swim out too far, since the depth drops off suddenly farther from shore.
During the rainy season and typhoon warnings, boat service stops and the island closes. Check whether it's operating before you set out.
The island gets very dark at night. Don't wander near the water or into the trees without a headlamp.
Some spots have sea urchins and sharp shells, so wear aqua shoes in the water.
Island rules set fixed times for fires, drinking, and noise, so follow the management's guidance.
The sand gets very hot at midday and UV exposure is strong. Rest in the shade and drink water often between
11 AM and 3 PM
